chapters.title: Mastering the Secrets of Nonverbal Communication
chapters.keys: Navarro says you can learn to read people, and most of what people communicate is nonverbal, so train yourself to watch. He gives his Ten Commandments for observing in this order: be an alert observer of your surroundings; read behavior in context; learn the universal signals everyone shows; learn each person's idiosyncratic signals, the habits unique to them; establish a baseline, how the person normally acts when at ease; look for clusters of tells, a tell being a behavior that reveals what someone thinks or feels; watch for changes in behavior, which signal changes in thought, feeling or intent; learn to spot false or misleading signals; separate comfort from discomfort; and observe discreetly. He says several tells read together against a baseline are more accurate than one gesture read alone. This week, watch the people you live and work with to learn how they normally act before you judge anything they do. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: police officer McFadden watched men whose behavior showed they were sizing up a store to commit a crime, and his observations became the basis of the 1968 Supreme Court ruling in Terry v. Ohio, which lets police stop and frisk someone whose behavior shows intent to commit a crime.

chapters.title: Living Our Limbic Legacy
chapters.keys: Read the limbic system, the part of the brain that reacts instantly and without thought, because Navarro calls it the honest brain, while the neocortex, the thinking brain, is the part that can lie. Its reactions come in his order: freeze, going still when threatened so as not to be noticed; flight, getting away or blocking, such as closing or covering the eyes, leaning away, or putting an object between yourself and the other person; and fight, aggression, which today shows up as arguing, insults and invading someone's space. After stress people use pacifying behaviors, self-touches that calm them: rubbing the neck, face or hair, stroking the legs, puffing out the cheeks and exhaling, or pulling the collar away from the neck, which he calls ventilating. He calls neck touching one of the most telling pacifiers: men tend to grip or rub the neck, women tend to cover the neck dimple, the hollow at the base of the throat. When a pacifier shows up right after a question or event, take it as a sign that something just caused discomfort. He says limbic reactions are honest because they are hardwired for survival and fire before we can think to hide them. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: agents looking for a fugitive questioned a woman at a house, and each time she was asked whether he could be inside she covered her neck dimple while saying no; the agents searched and found him there.

chapters.title: Getting a Leg Up on Body Language: Nonverbals of the Feet and Legs
chapters.keys: Watch the feet and legs, because Navarro calls them the most honest part of the body. His reason: people are taught to control their faces but pay little attention to their feet, which were built to react to danger. His signs: happy feet, feet that jiggle or bounce when someone is pleased; feet turning away, which signals a wish to leave; the knee clasp, hands on both knees with weight shifting forward, a sign the person wants to end the meeting; gravity-defying feet, rising onto the toes or lifting the feet, a sign of good feeling; standing with legs crossed, a sign of comfort, since people do not put themselves off balance near someone they distrust; leg splay, a wide stance that claims territory and can come before a confrontation; and freezing, locking the ankles or wrapping the feet around chair legs, a freeze response under stress. If you walk up to two people and they turn only their upper bodies toward you while their feet stay pointed at each other, they would rather you did not join. Watch for sudden changes in foot behavior, such as jiggling that suddenly stops, against the person's baseline. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: Torso Tips: Nonverbals of the Torso, Hips, Chest, and Shoulders
chapters.keys: People lean toward what they like and away from what they dislike, so read the torso for comfort and discomfort. Ventral fronting means turning the belly and chest toward someone you like; ventral denial means turning them away, a sign of discomfort or dislike. Torso shielding means covering the front with the arms, a bag, a jacket or another object when feeling insecure. Torso splay, sprawling out in a chair, shows comfort, but in a serious exchange such as being reprimanded it shows disrespect. Puffing out the chest and taking off a shirt are fight signals that can come before a confrontation. A full shrug, both shoulders rising high, goes with an honest I don't know, while a partial or one-shoulder shrug suggests the person is not committed to what they say; shoulders rising toward the ears while the head sinks, which he calls the turtle effect, shows insecurity and a wish to hide. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: Knowledge Within Reach: Nonverbals of the Arms
chapters.keys: Watch the arms, because Navarro says they react honestly to how we feel and to threats. Gravity-defying arms, raised high, show joy and excitement; arms pulled in close or held still show distress, and people restrict arm movement when afraid, scolded or holding something back. Arms held behind the back, which he calls the regal stance, signal higher status and a wish not to be touched. Arms akimbo, hands on hips with elbows out, is a territorial display, a claim on space and authority; the hooding effect, hands laced behind the head while leaning back, shows comfort and dominance, usually by whoever is in charge. Spreading the arms across chairs or a table also claims territory. He suggests using arms akimbo yourself, women in meetings especially, to show you will not be pushed around. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: Getting a Grip: Nonverbals of the Hands and Fingers
chapters.keys: Keep your hands where people can see them when you talk, because Navarro says people distrust a speaker whose hands are hidden, such as under a table. Don't point your finger at people; he says they find it offensive. Steepling, touching the fingertips of both hands together like a church steeple, signals high confidence; hand wringing and interlaced fingers rubbing against each other signal stress. Thumbs show confidence: thumbs up or sticking out of the pockets signal high confidence, while thumbs tucked into the pockets with the fingers outside signal low confidence. Hands that suddenly go still, or start to tremble, mark a change in feeling worth noting against the person's baseline. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.

chapters.title: The Mind's Canvas: Nonverbals of the Face
chapters.keys: Read the face carefully, because Navarro says it is the part people most learn to control and fake. His honest signs: lip compression, lips pressed together until they disappear, under stress; lip pursing, lips puckered, when someone disagrees or is weighing an alternative; the sneer, a sign of contempt; eye blocking, closing, covering or shielding the eyes when hearing something unwelcome; squinting or narrowing the eyes at something disliked; arched eyebrows, a gravity-defying sign of good feeling; and a wrinkled nose for disgust. Tell a real smile, which reaches the eyes, from a social smile, which only moves the mouth. He says looking away is not a sign of lying, because people look away to think. Check what the face shows against the rest of the body. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: a spy who was cooperating would not name the people who had worked with him, so investigators showed him 32 cards, each with a name; at two of the names his pupils narrowed and he squinted slightly, and the two people named later confessed.

chapters.title: Detecting Deception: Proceed with Caution!
chapters.keys: Proceed with caution: Navarro says catching a lie is very hard, and research shows even professionals do little better than a coin toss. Don't hunt for the lie itself; read comfort against discomfort, because honest people tend to show comfort and deceivers tend to show discomfort. His steps: create a relaxed setting, establish the person's baseline, ask your questions and note where discomfort rises, and look for synchrony, whether words and body agree, such as a yes with a nodding head, and emphasis, since truthful people stress their points with their hands and gravity-defying gestures and deceivers tend not to. Watch also for pacifying, arm restriction and ventral denial right after a question. Don't question in an accusing way, because your own manner can create discomfort that looks like guilt. Reversal: he says discomfort alone does not prove deception, since honest people under suspicion or stress show the same signs, so a sign of discomfort means look closer, not that you have found a liar. Story the author tells: none recalled with confidence.
